content: Schistosoma mansoni is a parasitic infection prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Chronic and advanced stages of the disease can manifest as abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood in the stool, liver cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and premature death. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of antischistosomal drugs, either used alone or in combination, for treating S. mansoni infections. The study involved a systematic search of databases including MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, and mRCT up to October 2012. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing antischistosomal drugs to placebo, other drugs, or varying doses of the same drug were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were conducted by one author and independently verified by another. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 52 trials involving 10,269 participants were included in the analysis. The quality of evidence ranged from moderate to low due to methodological limitations and small sample sizes in the trials. Praziquantel Praziquantel at a dose of 40 mg/kg likely reduces parasitological treatment failure one month after treatment compared to placebo (RR 3.13, 95% CI 1.03 to 9.53; two trials, 414 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Lower doses, such as 30 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg, appear to be less effective (RR 1.52, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.01; three trials, 521 participants; low-quality evidence and RR 2.23, 95% CI 1.64 to 3.02; two trials, 341 participants; low-quality evidence, respectively). Higher doses, up to 60 mg/kg, do not seem to provide additional benefits (four trials, 783 participants; moderate-quality evidence). The parasitological cure rate with 40 mg/kg of praziquantel varied significantly across studies, ranging from 52% in Senegal (1993) to 92% in Brazil (2006/2007). Oxamniquine Oxamniquine at a dose of 40 mg/kg likely reduces parasitological treatment failure at three months compared to placebo (RR 8.74, 95% CI 3.74 to 20.43; two trials, 82 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Lower doses, such as 30 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg, are likely less effective at one month (RR 1.78, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.75; four trials, 268 participants; low-quality evidence and RR 3.78, 95% CI 2.05 to 6.99; two trials, 190 participants; low-quality evidence, respectively). Higher doses, such as 60 mg/kg, do not show consistent benefits (four trials, 317 participants; low-quality evidence). These trials are over 20 years old, and limited information was available regarding their design and methodology. Praziquantel versus Oxamniquine Only one small trial directly compared praziquantel 40 mg/kg with oxamniquine 40 mg/kg, and the evidence was insufficient to determine which drug is more effective in reducing parasitological failure (one trial, 33 participants; very low-quality evidence). Ten additional trials compared oxamniquine at doses of 20, 30, and 60 mg/kg with praziquantel 40 mg/kg, but no significant differences in failure rates or egg reduction were observed. Combination Treatments The evidence is uncertain regarding whether combining praziquantel with artesunate reduces treatment failures compared to praziquantel alone at one month (one trial, 75 participants; very low-quality evidence). Two trials evaluated combinations of praziquantel and oxamniquine at different doses but found no statistically significant differences in failure rates (two trials, 87 participants). Other Outcomes and Adverse Events In trials assessing clinical improvement, no dose-dependent effects were observed for praziquantel or oxamniquine at lower doses (20 mg/kg and 30 mg/kg) compared to the standard 40 mg/kg. Symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood in stool, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly showed no significant differences in resolution at follow-ups conducted at one, three, six, 12, and 24 months (three trials, 655 participants). Adverse events were generally minor and transient but were not well-reported. Additional analyses revealed higher treatment failure rates with 40 mg/kg of both praziquantel and oxamniquine in children compared to adults. Conclusions Praziquantel at a dose of 40 mg/kg remains the standard treatment for S. mansoni infection, supported by the available evidence. Oxamniquine, though less commonly used, also appears effective. Further research is needed to optimize dosing regimens for children. Combination therapies targeting different developmental stages of the parasite and employing drugs with unrelated mechanisms of action should be explored in future studies.
